source_text: Cum vero praescribitur nemini sine Baptismo competere salutem, ex illa maxime pronuntiatione Domini, qui ait: Nisi natus ex aqua quis erit, non habet vitam, suboriuntur scrupulosi, imo temerarii retractatus quorumdam, quomodo ex ista praescriptione Apostolis salus competat, quos tinctos non invenimus in Domino, praeter Paulum. Imo cum Paulus solus ex illis Baptismum Christi induerit, aut praejudicatum esse de caeterorum periculo, qui careant aqua Christi, ut praescriptio salva sit, aut rescindi praescriptionem, si etiam non tinctis salus statuta est. Audivi, Domino teste, ejusmodi, ne quis me tam perditum existimet, ut ultro exagitem libidine styli, quae aliis scrupulum incutiant. Et nunc illis, ut potero, respondebo, qui negant Apostolos tinctos. Nam si humanum Joannis Baptismum inierant, et dominicum desiderabant quatenus unum Baptismum definierat ipse Dominus, dicens Petro perfundi nolenti: Qui semel lavit, non habet necesse rursum: quod utique non tincto non omnino dixisset: et haec est probatio exserta adversus illos, qui adimunt Apostolis etiam Joannis Baptismum, ut destruant aquae sacramentum. An credibile videri potest, in his personis viam tunc Domini praeparatam, id est Baptismum Joannis, quae ad viam Domini per totum orbem aperiendam destinabantur? Ipse Dominus, nullius poenitentiae debitor, tinctus est, peccatoribus non fuit necesse? Quid ergo? alii tincti non sunt? non tamen comites Christi, sed aemuli fidei, legis doctores et Pharisaei. Unde et suggeritur, cum adversantes Domino tingui noluerint, eos qui Dominum sequebantur, tinctos fuisse, nec cum aemulis suis sapuisse, maxime quando Dominus cui adhaerebant, testimonio Joannem extulisset, nemo, dicens, major inter natos foeminarum Joanne baptizatore. Alii plane satis coacte injiciunt tunc apostolos Baptismi vicem implesse cum in navicula fluctibus aspersi operti sunt; ipsum quoque Petrum per mare ingredientem satis mersum. Ut opinor autem, aliud aspergi vel intercipi violentia maris, aliud tingui disciplina religionis. Caeterum navicula illa figuram Ecclesiae praeferebat, quod in mari, id est saeculo, fluctibus, id est persecutionibus et tentationibus inquietatur Domino per patientiam velut dormiente, donec orationibus Sanctorum in ultimis suscitatus, compescat saeculum et tranquillitatem suis reddat. Nunc sive tincti quoquo modo fuerunt, sive illoti perseveraverunt, ut et illud dictum Domini, de uno lavacro sub Petri persona ad nos tantummodo spectet, de salute tamen Apostolorum satis temerarium est aestimare, quia illis vel primae allectionis, et exinde individuae familiaritatis praerogativa compendium Baptismi conferre posset. Cum illo, opinor, sequebantur illum, qui credenti cuique salutem pollicebatur: Fides tua te, aiebat, salvum fecit, et: Remittuntur tibi peccata, credenti utique, nec tamen tincto. Id si Apostolis defuit, nescio quorum fides: uno verbo Domini suscitatus teloneum dereliquit; patrem, et navem, et artem qua vitam sustentabat, deseruit; patris exequias despexit: summum illud Domini praeceptum: Qui patrem aut matrem mihi praetulerit, non est me dignus, ante perfecit quam audivit.
pass_a_gloss: But when it is prescribed that no one can attain salvation without Baptism, from that very pronouncement of the Lord, who says: Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life, there arise scrupulous, or rather reckless, objections of certain people, as to how from this prescription salvation can be applicable to the Apostles, whom we do not find to have been baptized in the Lord, except for Paul. Indeed, since Paul alone of them put on the Baptism of Christ, either the judgment about the danger of the others who lack the water of Christ must be prejudged, so that the prescription may be saved, or the prescription must be rescinded, if salvation is also established for those who are not baptized. I have heard, with the Lord as witness, such things, lest anyone think me so lost as to voluntarily stir up with the lust of my pen what inspires scruples in others. And now I will respond to those, as I can, who deny that the Apostles were baptized. For if they had undergone the human Baptism of John, and desired the Lord's, inasmuch as the Lord Himself had defined one Baptism, saying to Peter, who was unwilling to be washed: He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again, which He would certainly not have said to one who was not baptized; and this is the evident proof against those who deny the Apostles even the Baptism of John, so that they may destroy the sacrament of water. Can it be believed that, among those persons who were then preparing the way of the Lord, that is, the Baptism of John, which was destined to open the way of the Lord throughout the whole world, they did not undergo it? The Lord Himself, who owed no penance, was baptized; was it not necessary for sinners? What then? Were others not baptized? Not, however, the companions of Christ, but the rivals of faith, the teachers of the law, and the Pharisees. Whence it is also suggested that, when those who opposed the Lord were unwilling to be baptized, those who followed the Lord were baptized, and did not have the same opinion as their rivals, especially when the Lord, to whom they adhered, extolled John by testimony, saying: No one is greater among those born of women than John the Baptist. Others plainly force the idea that the Apostles then fulfilled the role of Baptism when they were sprinkled and covered by the waves in the boat; and that Peter also was sufficiently immersed when he entered the sea. But, in my opinion, it is one thing to be sprinkled or intercepted by the violence of the sea, and another to be baptized by the discipline of religion. Moreover, that boat represented the figure of the Church, which is troubled in the sea, that is, the world, by waves, that is, persecutions and temptations, while the Lord is asleep, as it were, through patience, until, having been aroused by the prayers of the Saints in the last times, He restrains the world and gives tranquility to His own. Now, whether they were baptized in some way or remained unbaptized, and whether that saying of the Lord, about one washing, under the person of Peter, pertains only to us, it is nevertheless very reckless to estimate the salvation of the Apostles, because they could have had the privilege of Baptism conferred upon them by the prerogative of their first election, and from then on, their individual familiarity. For they followed Him, who promised salvation to each believer, saying: Your faith has saved you, and: Your sins are forgiven, certainly to the believer, and not necessarily to the baptized. If the Apostles lacked this, I do not know what their faith was; with one word of the Lord, the tax collector arose and left his office; he deserted his father, and his boat, and the skill by which he sustained his life; he despised his father's funeral: he fulfilled that greatest commandment of the Lord, He who prefers his father or mother to me is not worthy of me, before he heard it.

choices.why: the context requires the meaning of Baptism
the phrase refers to the practice of Baptism as a religious ritual
the phrase indicates the Lord's patience during the troubles of the Church

bible_refs.note: Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life

pass_b_english: When it is laid down that no one can attain salvation without baptism, the rule rests on the Lord's own pronouncement: "Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life" (John 3:5). From that very text certain people raise scrupulous -- or rather reckless -- objections: how can the prescription apply to the apostles, whom we do not find baptized in the Lord except for Paul? Since Paul alone of them "put on the baptism of Christ," either the danger of the others who lack Christ's water must be prejudged so the rule stands, or the rule must be rescinded if salvation is also established for the unbaptized. I have heard such talk, with the Lord as my witness, so that no one may think me so lost as to voluntarily stir up scruples in others by a lust for writing. Now I will answer, as best I can, those who deny the apostles were baptized.

If they underwent the human baptism of John and desired the Lord's, since the Lord himself defined one baptism by telling Peter, who resisted washing, "He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again" (Matthew 3:14-15) -- words he certainly would not have spoken to an unbaptized man -- this is evident proof against those who strip the apostles even of John's baptism in order to destroy the sacrament of water. Can it be believed that the very persons destined to open the Lord's way throughout the world -- the way that was John's baptism -- did not undergo it? The Lord himself, who owed no repentance, was baptized; was it not necessary for sinners? What then? Were others baptized? Not the companions of Christ, but the rivals of faith, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees. Hence it is also suggested that when the Lord's opponents refused baptism, those who followed him were baptized and did not share their rivals' mind, especially when the Lord to whom they clung extolled John with the testimony: "No one is greater among those born of women than John the Baptist" (Matthew 11:11).

Others crudely force the idea that the apostles then fulfilled baptism's role when they were sprinkled and covered by waves in the boat, and that Peter was sufficiently immersed when he walked on the sea. But in my judgment it is one thing to be sprinkled or overtaken by the violence of the sea, another to be baptized by the discipline of religion. Besides, that boat represented the figure of the Church, tossed in the sea -- the world -- by waves of persecution and temptation while the Lord seems asleep through patience, until, roused by the prayers of the saints in the last times, he restrains the world and gives his own tranquility.

Now, whether they were baptized in some way or remained unbaptized, and whether the Lord's saying about one washing, spoken in Peter's person, pertains only to us, it is nevertheless very reckless to pronounce on the apostles' salvation. For they could have received the privilege of baptism by the prerogative of their first election and their subsequent intimate familiarity with him. They followed the one who promised salvation to every believer, saying: "Your faith has saved you" and "Your sins are forgiven" -- certainly to the believer, not necessarily to the baptized. If the apostles lacked this, I do not know what their faith was: at one word of the Lord the tax collector rose and left his booth; he deserted his father, his boat, and the trade that sustained his life; he despised his father's funeral; he fulfilled the Lord's supreme commandment -- "He who prefers father or mother to me is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:37) -- before he even heard it.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent version with correct scripture citations (John 3:5, Matthew 3:14-15, Matthew 11:11, Matthew 10:37) that match the quoted/alluded content. The distinction between 'sprinkled' (aspersi) and 'baptized' (tingui) is maintained. The theological nuances regarding the Apostles' salvation and the figure of the boat are preserved.
